content: The Japanese Red Cross Society (JRCS) is the sole organization authorized by the government of Japan to collect donated blood. Each blood collection center under JRCS must obtain permission from the Minister of Health, Labour, and Welfare. The Ministry of Public Health oversees accreditation processes, and facilities are required to comply with ISO 9001 and ISO 15189 standards. In Malaysia, the Department of Standards is responsible for licensing private healthcare facilities, and the Mauritius Standards Bureau certifies facilities under ISO 9001:2008. In Mexico, the Mexican Accreditation Body (Entidad Mexicana de Acreditación) oversees accreditation, while in Morocco, national blood centers are inspected annually, with audits conducted for all centers. New Zealand’s blood services are accredited by MedSafe, the national medicines regulatory authority, and certified under ISO 9001:2008. In the United States, the haemovigilance system is voluntary, and some transfusion services are accredited by the Joint Commission or the AABB. The Pacific Paramedical Training Centre (PPTC) offers a two-year distance learning program for a Diploma in Medical Laboratory Technology, which includes blood transfusion science. Any new blood transfusion structure must receive prior authorization from the Ministry of Health through the National Blood Transfusion Centre, which acts as both operator and guarantor of new facilities. In Serbia, two laboratories of the Blood Transfusion Institute of Serbia (BTIS) are accredited under SRPS ISO/IEC 17025, and one laboratory complies with European Federation of Immunogenetics (EFI) standards. The Novi Sad Blood Transfusion Institute’s HLA laboratory holds EFI accreditation. In South Africa, blood transfusion services are accredited by the South African National Accreditation System (SANAS). Sweden and Switzerland maintain comprehensive accreditation systems for blood services, adhering to ISO standards and European Commission directives. Globally, various organizations support blood transfusion services, including the World Health Organization (WHO), the Global Fund, the American Red Cross, and the Australian Red Cross. For example, in Cambodia, the Global Fund, PEPFAR, and the CDC provide support, while in Côte d’Ivoire, PEPFAR, WHO, and the Supply Chain Management System (SCMS) contribute to blood safety initiatives. In Ethiopia, the United States government, through PEPFAR and the CDC, collaborates with WHO to enhance blood transfusion services.
